course.title: Web Application Security
course.description: A practical, research-grounded course for understanding and assessing modern web applications. It covers HTTP and browser security controls, assessment methodology, authentication and authorization testing, injection and input validation, CSRF/SSRF/file-upload and business-logic issues, API and client-side security, configuration and supply-chain review, secure SDLC practices, professional reporting, retesting, and a self-contained local capstone. Offensive testing is constrained to authorized environments and paired with remediation and verification.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of IP networking, HTTP, and command-line use.
A local environment capable of running Python and a modern browser.
Only test systems and data you are explicitly authorized to assess.
learningOutcomes: Explain browser, HTTP, application, identity, and data-layer trust boundaries.
Plan an authorized web security assessment with scope and safe stop conditions.
Perform structured tests for authentication, authorization, sessions, input validation, and common web weaknesses.
Assess cookies, TLS, CORS, CSP, and related browser and transport controls.
Evaluate API object/function authorization, schema validation, resource-consumption controls, and client-side trust boundaries.
Review application configuration, secrets, dependencies, and secure-development controls.
Write reproducible security findings with impact, remediation, and retest criteria.
Complete a local end-to-end assessment and verify remediation with repeatable tests.

modules.title: Web Security Foundations and Testing Methodology
modules.description: Build the testing mindset: scope, trust boundaries, attack surface, evidence, and a repeatable security-testing lifecycle.

lessons.title: How Web Applications Work
lessons.description: Understand the browser, server, HTTP, sessions, APIs, and data stores well enough to locate security boundaries.
learningObjectives: Trace a browser-to-server request path.
Identify client-side and server-side trust boundaries.
Explain why HTTP semantics and application logic must be assessed separately.

notes.text: A web application typically combines browser code, HTTP requests/responses, server-side business logic, identity/session handling, and data services. Security failures often occur where assumptions change between these components.

items: Authentication answers who the requester is; authorization answers what that principal may do.
Client-side controls improve user experience but are not a trustworthy enforcement boundary.
Security testing should identify where untrusted input, identities, and privileges cross components.

notes.text:
GET /account/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.test
Accept: application/json

quiz.question: Which boundary must always be enforced server-side?
quiz.answer: Authorization
quiz.explanation: Server-side authorization is required because clients are not trusted.

summary: Web security starts with understanding data flow and trust boundaries.

lessons.title: Scope, Rules of Engagement, and Safe Testing
lessons.description: Plan an authorized assessment so testing is useful, reproducible, and non-destructive.
learningObjectives: Define in-scope and out-of-scope targets.
Specify test accounts, timing, rate limits, and escalation paths.
Explain why evidence and stop conditions belong in the rules of engagement.

notes.text: A professional web assessment begins before technical testing. Scope should identify applications, environments, domains, API hosts, accounts, excluded systems, test windows, and contact/escalation procedures.

items: Prefer staging or dedicated lab systems when possible.
Define prohibited actions such as destructive testing, production data changes, or uncontrolled load.
Document assumptions that could invalidate conclusions.

notes.text: Do not test systems you do not own or lack explicit authorization to assess.

quiz.question: What should be established before active security testing?
quiz.answer: Rules of engagement and scope
quiz.explanation: Authorized scope and test constraints reduce operational and legal risk.

summary: Authorization and scope are part of technical quality, not paperwork overhead.

lessons.title: Attack Surface Mapping and Information Gathering
lessons.description: Build a structured inventory of web entry points and application components without treating passive discovery as proof of a vulnerability.
learningObjectives: Inventory domains, hosts, endpoints, parameters, roles, and exposed functionality.
Differentiate passive reconnaissance from active testing.
Record evidence and confidence for discovered assets.

items: Map public-facing hosts, applications, APIs, authentication paths, upload features, admin interfaces, and third-party integrations.
Use application documentation, browser developer tools, proxy history, and authorized enumeration to build an attack-surface map.
Do not equate an exposed endpoint with a vulnerability; exposure becomes meaningful when behavior violates a security requirement.

notes.text:
Inventory example:
portal.example.test
api.example.test/v1
/admin
/upload
/oauth/callback

practicals.title: Map a Local Web Attack Surface
practicals.description: Create an evidence-backed inventory for a local training application.
steps: Read supplied application documentation and identify pages and API endpoints.
Record HTTP methods, parameters, roles, objects, and trust boundaries.
Mark evidence source and confidence for each item.
Turn the inventory into a prioritized test list.
practicals.solution: Produce a structured attack-surface table and prioritized test list.
practicals.output: A reproducible inventory suitable for driving later security tests.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct?
options: An endpoint is a vulnerability by definition
Discovery establishes what exists; testing determines whether security properties fail
A hidden endpoint is automatically safe
quiz.answer: Discovery establishes what exists; testing determines whether security properties fail
quiz.explanation: Inventory and vulnerability validation are distinct activities.

summary: A useful attack-surface map records evidence, not assumptions.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

lessons.title: Evidence, Reproducibility, and Reporting Basics
lessons.description: Learn how testers turn observations into defensible findings.
learningObjectives: Capture request/response evidence safely.
Write reproducible finding steps.
Separate fact, impact, and inference in a report.

items: A strong finding identifies affected component, precondition, exact steps, observed result, security impact, and remediation.
Redact secrets and unnecessary personal data from evidence.
Use timestamps and stable test identifiers when correlating evidence.

notes.text:
Finding structure:
Title
Asset
Precondition
Steps
Observed result
Impact
Evidence
Remediation

quiz.question: Which report element makes a finding easiest to verify?
quiz.answer: Reproducible steps with evidence
quiz.explanation: Repeatable steps and supporting evidence enable verification.

summary: Good reporting is part of testing accuracy.

tasks.title: Create an Assessment Scope Sheet
tasks.description: Draft a scope sheet for an authorized web application assessment.
tasks.problemStatement: Define target applications, exclusions, accounts, time window, allowed testing, evidence rules, and escalation contacts.
requirements: No software required; use a document or markdown file.
tasks.hint: Think about what would prevent an otherwise correct test from causing an operational incident.
tasks.solutionCode:
Example:
In scope: https://lab.example.test, api.lab.example.test
Out of scope: third-party IdP, production payments
Limits: no destructive actions, max 1 request/sec for active enumeration
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution is intentionally procedural because safe testing depends on context and authorization.

modules.title: HTTP, Browser Controls, and Transport Security
modules.description: Understand the protocol and browser security controls that web applications depend on.

lessons.title: HTTP Requests, Responses, Headers, and Methods
lessons.description: Read HTTP traffic precisely so application behavior can be tested rather than guessed.
learningObjectives: Interpret methods, status codes, headers, and body semantics.
Distinguish idempotent/read-oriented operations from state-changing workflows.
Identify security-relevant headers.

notes.text:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: lab.example.test
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"alice","password":"example"}

items: Headers can affect caching, content handling, authentication context, and browser behavior.
Status codes communicate semantics but application-specific authorization decisions still need testing.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is normally used to request a resource representation without asking the server to change state?
quiz.answer: GET
quiz.explanation: GET is defined as retrieving a current representation of a target resource.

summary: HTTP knowledge is foundational to both manual and automated testing.

lessons.title: Cookies, Sessions, and Browser State
lessons.description: Assess session security across issuance, storage, rotation, expiration, and invalidation.
learningObjectives: Explain Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite cookie attributes.
Identify session fixation and session invalidation risks.
Test session behavior across login and privilege changes.

notes.text: Cookies commonly carry session identifiers. Secure limits transmission to secure channels; HttpOnly prevents document.cookie access by scripts in supporting browsers; SameSite controls cross-site sending behavior.

items: Regenerate session identifiers when privilege changes require it.
Expire sessions according to risk and operational needs.
Do not put sensitive authorization decisions only in browser-controlled state.

quiz.question: Which cookie attribute helps prevent JavaScript from reading the cookie value?
quiz.answer: HttpOnly
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly restricts access from document.cookie.

summary: Session security is a lifecycle property, not just a cookie flag.

lessons.title: TLS and Certificate Validation
lessons.description: Understand what HTTPS protects and how certificate validation affects endpoint authenticity.
learningObjectives: Explain TLS confidentiality and integrity at a high level.
Describe certificate-chain and hostname validation.
Recognize why TLS does not fix server-side application flaws.

notes.text: TLS creates a protected channel and authenticates the peer through certificate-based trust mechanisms. The application must still enforce authentication, authorization, input validation, and safe data handling.
Disabling certificate validation in clients can convert endpoint authentication into a trust-on-first-look or trust-anything model and should not be used as a general workaround.

quiz.question: What does TLS not guarantee by itself?
options: Correct authorization logic in the application
Integrity protection of the protected channel
quiz.answer: Correct authorization logic in the application
quiz.explanation: TLS protects transport; it does not enforce application business rules.

summary: Transport security and application security are complementary.

lessons.title: CORS, CSP, and Browser Security Headers
lessons.description: Learn how browser-enforced policies affect cross-origin requests and script/resource execution.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of CORS.
Explain how CSP restricts resource execution.
Identify insecure header configurations and test their effect.

items: CORS controls whether a browser may expose cross-origin response data to requesting scripts; it is not an authorization system.
CSP controls what a page may load or execute and can reduce XSS impact.
Security headers should be tested against the application’s actual behavior.

notes.text:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted.example.test

quiz.question: What is CORS primarily controlling?
quiz.answer: Browser access to cross-origin responses
quiz.explanation: CORS is a browser policy mechanism for controlled cross-origin sharing.

summary: Browser policy controls must be tested in context.

tasks.title: Review Browser Security Headers
tasks.description: Assess a fictional response-header set for common browser-security weaknesses.
tasks.problemStatement: Identify insecure or missing CSP, CORS, cookie, and transport-related controls and recommend corrected policies.
objectives: Explain compatibility trade-offs for each proposed control.
requirements: Use only the supplied response headers.
tasks.hint: Do not recommend a restrictive policy without considering the resources the application actually needs.
tasks.solutionCode: A good solution explains both the security benefit and the operational effect of each header.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task reinforces browser-side policy analysis rather than memorizing header names.

modules.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Session Testing
modules.description: Test the identity controls that protect accounts, roles, and sensitive operations.

lessons.title: Authentication Testing
lessons.description: Assess login, password policy, MFA, recovery, lockout, and error behavior.
learningObjectives: Test positive and negative authentication paths.
Identify account-enumeration and recovery weaknesses.
Evaluate MFA and reauthentication requirements for sensitive actions.

items: Authentication testing includes login, logout, password changes, reset flows, registration, and alternate authentication channels.
Error messages should avoid unnecessarily revealing whether an account exists.
Rate limiting and abuse controls need to be tested with safe, bounded traffic.

quiz.question: Which area belongs in authentication testing?
options: Login, recovery, password change, registration, and related identity flows
quiz.answer: Login, recovery, password change, registration, and related identity flows
quiz.explanation: Authentication is a lifecycle, not one endpoint.

summary: Test the complete identity lifecycle.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

lessons.title: Authorization and Access-Control Testing
lessons.description: Find horizontal and vertical privilege failures using role and object comparisons.
learningObjectives: Differentiate horizontal from vertical authorization failures.
Test object ownership and role boundaries.
Verify denial behavior at the server boundary.

items: Horizontal escalation involves access to another principal’s resources at a similar privilege level. Vertical escalation crosses role/privilege boundaries.
Authorization should be checked for each sensitive operation, not inferred from menu visibility.
Compare allowed and denied cases systematically.

notes.text:
Request A: GET /api/orders/1001 as user-A
Request B: GET /api/orders/1002 as user-A
Expected: user-A receives only authorized objects.

practicals.title: Test Object-Level Authorization
practicals.description: Compare allowed and denied object access using two fictional lab identities.
steps: Use the owner identity to request its object.
Use the peer identity to request the owner object.
Record expected and observed status codes and response bodies.
Document any authorization mismatch as a finding.
practicals.solution: Show that object authorization must be enforced server-side for each requested resource.
practicals.output: A before/after authorization matrix with evidence.

quiz.question: A user can access another customer’s record by changing an object ID. What class of issue is this?
quiz.answer: Horizontal authorization failure
quiz.explanation: The same user is reaching a peer user’s resource without permission.

summary: Authorization must be enforced on the requested resource and action.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

lessons.title: Session Fixation and Session Lifecycle
lessons.description: Test whether session identifiers remain safe across authentication and privilege changes.
learningObjectives: Explain session fixation.
Test session rotation and invalidation.
Check concurrent session behavior where relevant.

notes.text: Session fixation occurs when an attacker can cause a victim to authenticate using a session identifier the attacker already knows. A common defense is to issue a new session identifier after successful authentication or privilege changes.

Test sequence:
1. Obtain pre-auth session cookie.
2. Authenticate.
3. Compare session identifier.
Expected: identifier changes when the application requires rotation.

quiz.question: What is the central defense against session fixation?
options: Keeping the same session ID after login
Rotating the session identifier at the appropriate authentication boundary
quiz.answer: Rotating the session identifier at the appropriate authentication boundary
quiz.explanation: Rotation breaks the attacker’s knowledge of the pre-auth session identifier.

summary: Session identifiers need lifecycle controls.

lessons.title: MFA, Recovery, and Sensitive Actions
lessons.description: Evaluate stronger authentication requirements around account recovery and high-impact operations.
learningObjectives: Identify high-risk account recovery paths.
Explain why MFA reset flows can bypass strong primary authentication.
Test reauthentication requirements for sensitive changes.

items: Account recovery is an authentication path and must be protected accordingly.
Sensitive actions such as changing MFA factors, recovery addresses, or payment details may justify reauthentication or step-up authentication.
Security questions are generally weak when answers are guessable or publicly knowable.

quiz.question: Why must MFA reset be tested separately from normal login?
options: It is not part of security
Recovery can become an alternate path around stronger authentication
quiz.answer: Recovery can become an alternate path around stronger authentication
quiz.explanation: A weaker recovery path can negate a stronger primary flow.

summary: Strong authentication can be undermined by weak recovery or step-up controls.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

tasks.title: Design an Authorization Test Matrix
tasks.description: Create a matrix to test role and ownership boundaries for an application with viewer, editor, and admin roles.
tasks.problemStatement: Build cases for allowed and denied access to records and administrative functions, including object-ownership changes.
requirements: Use a controlled lab or fictional scenario appropriate to the task.
tasks.hint: Vary one authorization dimension at a time so a failure is attributable.
tasks.solutionCode: Example rows: viewer reads own report=allow; viewer reads another user report=deny; editor deletes user account=deny; admin changes role=allow.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A matrix makes authorization testing systematic and repeatable.

modules.title: Input Validation and Injection
modules.description: Learn to identify interpreter-boundary failures while using safe, non-destructive lab techniques.

lessons.title: SQL Injection and Parameterized Queries
lessons.description: Understand how untrusted input can become SQL code and how parameterization separates data from syntax.
learningObjectives: Explain SQL injection at the query-construction level.
Recognize vulnerable string concatenation.
Verify parameterized query behavior in code review and testing.

notes.text:
# Vulnerable pattern (do not deploy)
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + username + "'"

# Safer parameterized pattern
cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', (username,))
Use controlled lab data for injection exercises. Do not probe production databases without explicit authorization.

practicals.title: Verify Parameterized SQLite Queries
practicals.description: Practice safe data binding against an in-memory SQLite database.
steps: Create an in-memory SQLite database and users table.
Insert two fictional users with parameterized statements.
Query by a user-provided name using a parameter marker.
Explain why the input remains data rather than SQL syntax.
practicals.solution:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)")
conn.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", [(1, "alice"), (2, "bob")])
name = "alice"
print(conn.execute("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchone())
practicals.output: The query returns the matching row without constructing SQL from the input string.

quiz.question: What is the primary protection against SQL injection in database APIs?
quiz.answer: Parameterized queries
quiz.explanation: Parameterization keeps user data separate from SQL syntax.

summary: Treat database statements as code/data boundaries.

resources.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

lessons.title: XSS: Reflected, Stored, and DOM-Based
lessons.description: Understand cross-site scripting variants and context-aware defenses.
learningObjectives: Differentiate reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS.
Choose context-appropriate output encoding.
Explain CSP as a defense layer rather than a primary fix.

items: Reflected XSS occurs when input is returned in a response; stored XSS persists in application data; DOM-based XSS arises from unsafe client-side data flow.
Output encoding must match the context where data is inserted.
HTML sanitization and safe templating can help in contexts where HTML is intentionally allowed.

notes.text:
Safe principle:
Treat user content as data, not executable markup.
Use a framework/template system with contextual escaping by default.

quiz.question: Why is context-specific output encoding important for XSS defense?
quiz.answer: Different contexts interpret characters differently
quiz.explanation: HTML, attribute, script, URL, and CSS contexts have different parsers and rules.

summary: XSS defenses depend on the output context.

resources.title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

lessons.title: Command and Template Injection
lessons.description: Recognize dangerous interpreter boundaries beyond SQL and HTML.
learningObjectives: Identify command-injection patterns.
Explain why shell invocation is risky with untrusted input.
Choose allowlist validation and safe APIs where possible.

items: Command injection occurs when application-controlled data changes the meaning of a command interpreter invocation.
Prefer APIs that accept structured arguments without a shell.
If an operation requires a limited set of values, validate against an allowlist.

notes.text:
Preferred pattern:
subprocess.run(["convert", input_path, output_path], check=True)
Avoid building a shell command string from untrusted data.

quiz.question: Which design most reduces shell-command injection risk?
options: Concatenate strings into a shell command
Use structured process APIs without a shell when possible
quiz.answer: Use structured process APIs without a shell when possible
quiz.explanation: Structured arguments reduce the chance that data is interpreted as shell syntax.

summary: Interpreter boundaries should be explicit and narrow.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

lessons.title: Path Traversal and File Handling
lessons.description: Test whether user-controlled paths can escape intended directories or access unintended files.
learningObjectives: Explain path traversal conceptually.
Use canonicalization and allowlists safely.
Design file-storage paths that do not depend directly on user input.

notes.text:
Safer design idea:
base_dir = Path("/srv/app/uploads")
file_id = lookup_server_side_identifier(request_id)
path = base_dir / file_id
# Do not derive file_id directly from a raw user path.
Do not use traversal payloads against real systems without explicit authorization.

quiz.question: Which design is safest for stored files?
options: Map user-controlled IDs to server-side known file paths
Store uploads in the application source directory
quiz.answer: Map user-controlled IDs to server-side known file paths
quiz.explanation: Server-side mapping reduces dependence on untrusted path strings.

summary: File operations need explicit containment and authorization.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

tasks.title: Review an Injection-Prone Handler
tasks.description: Analyze a fictional handler containing SQL and shell-construction risks and rewrite it using safer boundaries.
tasks.problemStatement: Replace string-built SQL and shell commands with parameterized or structured APIs and add validation.
objectives: Explain why validation is not a substitute for parameterization.
tasks.hint: Ask what part of the input is data and what part is executable syntax.
tasks.solutionCode: Use sqlite3 parameter substitution and subprocess.run with an argument list and shell=False.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution removes ambiguity at the interpreter boundary instead of attempting to sanitize arbitrary code syntax.

modules.title: CSRF, SSRF, File Uploads, and Business Logic
modules.description: Test application workflows where security failures arise from trust assumptions and business processes rather than one simple input parser.

lessons.title: CSRF and State-Changing Requests
lessons.description: Assess cross-site request risks for cookie-authenticated state changes.
learningObjectives: Explain CSRF conditions.
Test CSRF tokens and SameSite controls.
Differentiate CSRF from XSS and authorization failures.

items: CSRF relies on a victim’s browser carrying ambient authentication to a target site while an attacker induces a request.
Synchronizer tokens, double-submit patterns, SameSite cookies, and origin checks can contribute to defense depending on architecture.
APIs using bearer tokens in non-browser clients may have different CSRF properties.

quiz.question: Which condition is central to classic CSRF?
options: The browser automatically sends authentication context with a cross-site request
quiz.answer: The browser automatically sends authentication context with a cross-site request
quiz.explanation: Ambient authentication context is a key part of classic CSRF.

summary: CSRF testing must consider authentication transport and browser behavior.

resources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

lessons.title: SSRF and Server-Side Fetching
lessons.description: Understand how server-side URL fetching can cross security boundaries.
learningObjectives: Explain SSRF at the server-request layer.
Identify risky URL-fetch features such as webhooks and importers.
Describe allowlist and network-egress controls.

items: SSRF can cause a server to make requests the attacker cannot directly make, including requests to internal services when network placement allows it.
Prefer strict destination allowlists and validated protocols/ports.
Network controls should limit the blast radius of application-layer mistakes.

notes.text: Validate SSRF controls in isolated environments. Do not use internal-network targets you are not authorized to access.

quiz.question: What makes SSRF different from a client-side request?
options: The server performs the outbound request
quiz.answer: The server performs the outbound request
quiz.explanation: The security boundary is that the application server is induced to make the request.

summary: SSRF combines application validation with network egress control.

resources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

lessons.title: File Upload Security
lessons.description: Design and test upload features for content validation, storage isolation, and safe serving.
learningObjectives: Assess filename, type, size, and storage controls.
Explain why extension checks alone are insufficient.
Design safe storage and serving policies.

items: Validate uploads against business-appropriate type and size rules.
Store uploads outside executable application paths when architecture permits and use generated server-side names.
Serve user-uploaded content with safe content types and download semantics as appropriate.

quiz.question: Why should server-side generated filenames be preferred for uploads?
options: They reduce path and naming control from untrusted input
quiz.answer: They reduce path and naming control from untrusted input
quiz.explanation: Server-generated names reduce direct influence of untrusted path and filename components.

summary: Uploads create both input-validation and storage-boundary risks.

lessons.title: Business Logic Abuse and Workflow Testing
lessons.description: Find security problems that arise when individually valid actions can be combined into an invalid business outcome.
learningObjectives: Map critical workflows and invariants.
Design abuse cases around sequencing and state transitions.
Test server-side enforcement of business rules.

items: Business-logic testing asks whether the application preserves business invariants across a sequence of valid requests.
Examples include replaying one-time actions, changing workflow order, bypassing approval states, or manipulating quantity/price assumptions.
These flaws often require understanding expected business behavior rather than only technical syntax.

quiz.question: What is a business-logic vulnerability?
options: A valid sequence of operations that violates intended business rules
quiz.answer: A valid sequence of operations that violates intended business rules
quiz.explanation: Business logic flaws can involve technically valid requests producing an invalid business outcome.

summary: Model security around workflows and invariants, not only inputs.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

tasks.title: Build a Secure Upload Design
tasks.description: Design an upload workflow for a document portal with preview and download functions.
tasks.problemStatement: Specify validation, storage, naming, authorization, scanning hooks, and safe response headers.
objectives: Prevent path injection and unauthorized retrieval.
requirements: Keep malware scanning as an integration boundary; do not implement malware analysis.
tasks.hint: Treat the upload as untrusted data from ingestion through retrieval.
tasks.solutionCode: Use server-generated opaque IDs, store outside executable paths, authorize download per object, enforce size/type policy, and serve with safe content handling.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The design reduces both storage and retrieval risks while preserving an auditable workflow.

modules.title: API, Client-Side, and Modern Web Architecture Testing
modules.description: Extend testing into APIs, SPAs, GraphQL-like patterns, and client-side trust boundaries.

lessons.title: API Authorization and Object-Level Access
lessons.description: Test object and function-level authorization in APIs.
learningObjectives: Differentiate object-level and function-level authorization.
Test IDOR/BOLA-style cases in a controlled lab.
Check property-level data exposure.

items: OWASP API1:2023 describes broken object level authorization as a major API risk.
Test every sensitive object access with different principals and object IDs.
Property-level authorization matters when an endpoint returns fields a caller should not receive.

quiz.question: Which OWASP API category focuses on object identifiers and unauthorized access to individual objects?
quiz.answer: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization
quiz.explanation: API1 addresses authorization checks on object access.

summary: APIs require explicit object and function authorization.

lessons.title: API Schema, Rate Limits, and Resource Consumption
lessons.description: Assess API input schemas and abuse controls without generating uncontrolled load.
learningObjectives: Explain schema validation and content-type controls.
Assess bounded rate limiting.
Identify resource-intensive operations that require protection.

items: Rate limiting is one layer of protection for resource consumption and sensitive business flows.
Validate request structure before deep processing.
Use safe lab rates; do not conduct volumetric load testing against shared systems.

quiz.question: What is the main security purpose of rate limiting?
options: To reduce abuse and uncontrolled resource consumption
quiz.answer: To reduce abuse and uncontrolled resource consumption
quiz.explanation: Rate limiting constrains request frequency or cost but does not replace authorization.

summary: API availability and abuse controls must be tested within safe bounds.

lessons.title: Client-Side Security and DOM Trust Boundaries
lessons.description: Inspect browser code for unsafe sinks and assumptions about attacker-controlled data.
learningObjectives: Identify common DOM sinks conceptually.
Trace data from URL/storage/network into client-side rendering.
Explain why client-side validation cannot enforce authorization.

items: Client-side code handles attacker-influenced inputs such as URL fragments, query parameters, storage values, and API responses.
Unsafe DOM manipulation can create client-side XSS even when server responses are safe.
Authorization decisions must not depend only on JavaScript state.

quiz.question: Why is client-side role hiding insufficient for authorization?
options: Users can alter client state or call the server directly
quiz.answer: Users can alter client state or call the server directly
quiz.explanation: The server remains the authority for sensitive operations.

summary: Treat the browser as an untrusted execution environment.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG Web Application Security Testing

lessons.title: GraphQL and Structured API Considerations
lessons.description: Understand testing concerns unique to query-based APIs.
learningObjectives: Identify schema exposure and authorization risks.
Explain query-cost and depth controls.
Test field-level authorization and introspection assumptions in a lab.

items: GraphQL can expose many fields and nested relationships through a single endpoint, making authorization and resource-consumption analysis important.
Schema visibility does not equal authorization.
Query complexity controls can limit expensive nested operations.

quiz.question: Why can nested API queries require explicit cost controls?
options: A single request can trigger substantial server-side work
quiz.answer: A single request can trigger substantial server-side work
quiz.explanation: Nested queries can expand server-side computation and data access.

summary: Modern APIs concentrate security responsibility in resolver/data-access logic.

tasks.title: Create an API Authorization Test Plan
tasks.description: Create a test plan for an API exposing customer, invoice, and admin endpoints.
tasks.problemStatement: Test object ownership, role restrictions, field exposure, rate limits, and error behavior.
objectives: Cover at least six test cases.
Map at least two tests to OWASP API categories.
requirements: Use only fictional object IDs and test accounts.
tasks.hint: Vary principal, endpoint, method, object, and role independently.
tasks.solutionCode: A strong plan includes API1, API3, and API5 style cases with evidence fields.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan converts API security concepts into repeatable tests.

modules.title: Secure Configuration, Secrets, Dependencies, and DevSecOps
modules.description: Assess application configuration and software supply-chain controls throughout development and deployment.

lessons.title: Security Misconfiguration and Deployment Review
lessons.description: Find insecure defaults, debug exposure, excessive permissions, and unsafe deployment settings.
learningObjectives: Inspect configuration against a documented baseline.
Identify debug/admin exposure and unsafe defaults.
Explain configuration drift.

items: Configuration testing covers deployment, infrastructure integration, headers, error handling, admin interfaces, and unused functionality.
A secure baseline should be role- and environment-specific.
Avoid reporting a configuration as insecure without understanding its operational purpose and exposure.

quiz.question: Which is a strong approach to configuration assessment?
options: Compare actual settings to an approved security baseline
quiz.answer: Compare actual settings to an approved security baseline

project.name: Secure Web Application Assessment Capstone
project.description: Assess a deliberately structured local web application with a focus on object-level authorization, input validation, reporting quality, and retesting. All data is fictional and all requests remain on localhost.
steps: Create a local Python environment; no third-party package is required for the application.
Map endpoints and trust boundaries before testing.
Run the supplied test_app.py and record the baseline.
Compare owner and peer-object requests using the X-Lab-User identities.
Document any confirmed authorization or validation finding with reproducible evidence.
Apply the necessary remediation and keep the fix server-side.
Run the integration checks again and verify corrected behavior.
Produce a final report containing scope, methodology, findings, remediation, and retest evidence.

code.test_app.py:
import json
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def req(path, method="GET", body=None, user="alice"):
    data = None if body is None else json.dumps(body).encode()
    request = Request(f"http://127.0.0.1:8000{path}", data=data, method=method, headers={"X-Lab-User": user})
    if data is not None:
        request.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=2) as response:
            return response.status, json.loads(response.read())
    except HTTPError as exc:
        return exc.code, json.loads(exc.read())

server = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, str(ROOT / "app.py")])
try:
    time.sleep(0.6)
    assert req("/api/orders/1001", user="alice")[0] == 200
    assert req("/api/orders/1002", user="alice")[0] == 404
    assert req("/api/orders/1002", user="admin")[0] == 200
    assert req("/api/report", method="POST", body={"event":"login","severity":"unknown"})[0] == 400
    assert req("/api/report", method="POST", body={"event":"login","severity":"high"})[0] == 202
finally:
    server.terminate()
    server.wait(timeout=2)
code.README.md:
# Secure Web Application Assessment Capstone

This project is local-only and uses fictional in-memory data. The target is 127.0.0.1:8000.
Assess authorization and input validation, document evidence, and verify corrected behavior with the supplied test script.

project.explanation: The capstone uses only the Python standard library so it can be executed and validated offline. The primary security boundary is object-level authorization: the server must decide whether the authenticated lab principal may access the requested order. The report endpoint demonstrates input validation and safe failure behavior. The final assessment emphasizes method—scope, evidence, remediation, and verification—rather than uncontrolled exploitation.
